initial_presentation: A 10-year-old female presented with increasing difficulty in breathing and a productive cough 6 hours after arriving at Abha city, which is at an altitude of 2270 meters. The family resides in a low-altitude area at 525 meters. The patient had a history of fever, cough, and mild shortness of breath.

A previously healthy 12-year-old male was brought to the emergency department 7 days after ingesting an unknown quantity of a liquid. Post-ingestion, he experienced multiple episodes of vomiting, occasionally with bloody secretions. He appeared pale. His relatives reported no seizures. Over the past week, he had anorexia, lethargy, and general discomfort. Upon examination, he was drowsy but responsive, afebrile with a heart rate of 71/min, regular rhythm, blood pressure 100/75 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. His oral mucosa was congested and swollen, with exudative ulcerations on the tongue and swollen lips. Pupils were 2 mm bilaterally and reactive to light. Lung auscultation revealed clear lung fields. The pulse was 71 beats/min with a regular rhythm, and no extra heart sounds or murmurs were detected. On arrival, his blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg. Vital signs were stable with a body temperature of 37.7°C, pulse 71 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg. There were no neurological symptoms, organomegaly, tachycardia, or tachypnea. He received intravenous therapy, including IV fluids, antiemetic (ondansetron), and ranitidine as supportive measures.

A 49-year-old woman was transferred to our emergency room from another hospital for treatment of a brain tumor. Her main complaint was visual field disturbance, and she had experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure a week prior.

A 19-year-old female, first in birth order, born of a non-consanguineous marriage, was brought to the psychiatric outpatient department for behavioral issues over three years. Symptoms included repeated self-injurious behavior, lack of interest in activities, anger outbursts, irritability, mood fluctuations, and excessive social media usage along with alcohol and cannabis consumption. Her academic performance declined, and she engaged in multiple short-term relationships. She exhibited intense emotional fluctuations, anger outbursts, hostility towards teachers and family members, and multiple episodes of self-harming behavior like consuming phenyl or excess medicines when her demands were not met. She reported feeling empty and emotionally numb, resorting to social media to make friends. She eventually started consuming alcohol and cannabis, dropped out of college in the 11th grade, and engaged in high-risk behavior for thrill and novelty. She expressed a strong desire to dye her hair a bright color, get multiple tattoos, visit haunted houses, and engage in other thrilling activities. Her developmental history included normal milestones with average academic performance. Her mother separated from her father when she was around three years old due to his alcohol use and anti-social traits. Her relationship with her mother and younger brother was strained due to constant comparison between the two by the mother. She attained menarche at 13 years of age and had regular menstrual cycles. Physical examination revealed short stature for her age, with a height of 145 cm and a weight of 31.5 kg. She had sparse eyebrows, pigmentation over eyelids, dry and dull facial skin, a pinched nose, mild prognathism with overcrowding of teeth and bleeding gums, sparse dry and thin hair on the scalp, lack of secondary sexual characteristics, lack of axillary hair, thin dry wrinkled skin with mottling over arms, hands, feet, and abdomen with visible blood vessels, and rough ridges over the nails. Her mother noticed she was not growing like other girls her age but did not seek medical advice due to her work commitments and the absence of physical symptoms. She was unaware of the patient's skin condition. On mental status examination, the patient was well-kempt, cooperative, and communicative. She reported her mood as low, while her affect was stable and congruent to mood. She did not exhibit delusions, hallucinations, or suicidal ideations. Her judgment was preserved, and she had no insight into her condition.

A 30-year-old woman who had recently given birth was admitted to the hospital with a headache and nausea that started 24 hours earlier. Neurological examination revealed visual disturbance occurring just before the headache began. Motor and sensory functions in both upper and lower extremities were normal.

A 55-year-old male presented with a recurring, itchy rash on the scalp, forehead, face, and neck for the past seven years. Initially, the rash appeared as linearly distributed papules on the right side of the forehead and remained stable for about five years without symptoms, leading to no medical consultation. Over time, the rash spread in a linear pattern to the right side of the face, neck, and scalp, as well as the left side of the forehead and neck. The patient reported itching and noted that the lesions worsened with sun exposure. Hair loss was observed in the affected scalp areas. There was no family history of similar lesions. Physical examination revealed hyperkeratotic, skin-colored to hyperpigmented papules, both grouped and scattered, arranged in a linear pattern on the right forehead, right cheek, and left forehead. Some lesions had a violaceous hue but lacked whitish streaks on the surface. A similar pattern was observed on the right side of the neck. The lesions were not associated with erythema or scaling. Additional examination of the scalp revealed a few hyperkeratotic papulonodular eruptions on the vertex, with surrounding skin showing pigmented macules and slight atrophy, along with hair loss. Nail and oral mucosa examinations were normal.

A 62-year-old male presented with a history of developing a small number of papular lesions on his trunk 12 months prior. Over time, he progressively developed hundreds of elevated, brownish papular lesions across his body. These lesions were neither painful nor itchy. Some papules resolved spontaneously, but new lesions continued to appear. There were no precipitating factors and no other systemic issues. General medical examination showed no abnormalities. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly on palpation. Cutaneous examination revealed a widespread papular eruption on the face, trunk, and proximal parts of the arms and legs, with the scalp, palms, and soles being spared. Mucous membranes were not involved. The individual lesions were non-confluent, hemispherical, and ranged from skin-colored to brown papules, measuring 3 to 8 mm in size; some had central umblication, resembling molluscum contagiosum. The patient reported spontaneous regression of some lesions, with focal residual hyperpigmentation at the sites of resolution. The eruption was asymptomatic.

The patient is a 19-year-old woman who was born full-term to a non-consanguineous couple. At birth, she exhibited low muscle tone, and her breathing and crying were weak. During her first month of life, she experienced respiratory failure and required a tracheotomy and mechanical ventilation. Throughout infancy, her muscle weakness persisted; however, she achieved all motor developmental milestones on time. She also experienced intermittent cyanosis due to a patent ductus arteriosus and underwent corrective heart surgery at the age of 2.

A 61-year-old, right-handed male experienced a sudden alteration in mental status following a notable decline in functionality over the past 2 years. Previously, he was highly functional and held an executive position at a Fortune 500 company. The change in mental status included several behavioral alterations such as cruelty toward family members and pets, promiscuity, adultery, drug abuse, excessive spending, and a lack of empathy. His family also observed changes in his speech patterns, specifically in phonation and pronunciation of words. Initially, he was treated for bipolar disorder but did not respond to mood-stabilizing medications. After losing his job, he was admitted to the psychiatric ward due to suicidal tendencies.

A 34-year-old male, seven years and three months post-kidney transplantation, presented in February 2016 with symptoms including reduced appetite, weight loss, visible blood in urine, fatigue, and significantly reduced urine output (less than 200 mL). The patient had received a living kidney transplant from his 41-year-old mother on November 27, 2008, after two months of hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The transplanted kidney was placed in the right iliac fossa.
